SESSION 01 
Introduction to Version Control Systems, Git, 
and GitHub 
 
Overview 
This session provides a concise overview of Version Control Systems (VCS), 
focusing on Git, and GitHub. It covers the history and types of VCS, the purpose 
of Git and GitHub, and steps for Git installation. Additionally, it includes 
instructions for setting up a GitHub account, creating a repository, and using 
the GitHub Web interface to add and commit files. This foundation is essen tial 
for managing projects effectively, such as organizing tasks in a well-structured 
CRM system. 
 
Learning Objectives 
In this session, students will learn to: 
● Outline the evolution of Version Control Systems (VCS) 
● Classify different types of VCS 
● Define Git and GitHub 
● Explain the significance of Git and GitHub in version control 
● Explain the installation of Git and Git Desktop  
● Illustrate how to create a GitHub account 
● Explain basic repository actions using Git and GitHub 
 
Introduction to Version Control Systems (VCS) 
 
Version control, often referred to as source control, is the practice of monitoring 
and managing changes to software code. VCS are tools that assist software 
teams in managing code alterations over time. With the acceleration of 
development environments, t hese systems enable teams to work more 

© Aptech Limited 
 
efficiently and intelligently. They are particularly advantageous for DevOps 
teams, as they help decrease development time and improve the success of 
deployments. 
 
 
Importance of Tracking Changes in Software Development 
 
Tracking changes in software development is crucial for ensuring seamless 
collaboration and maintaining accountability. VCS such as Git enable multiple 
developers to work on a project simultaneously without overwriting each 
other's work.  
 
 
 
VCS provide mechanisms to resolve conflicts efficiently. They maintain a 
comprehensive history of changes, including who made them and when.  
 
This history is essential for understanding the project's evolution and for 
debugging. VCS also serve as a backup, allowing recovery of previous versions 
in case of data loss or corruption. By facilitating branching, developers can 
experiment with new feat ures without affecting the main codebase. This 
encourages innovation. Code review processes integrated with VCS improve 
code quality and foster knowledge sharing. Continuous integration tools 
ensure that new code does not break existing functionality. Mean ingful 
commit messages and changelogs serve as documentation, helping current 
and future developers understand the codebase.  
 
VCS provide a transparent record of changes necessary for compliance and 

© Aptech Limited 
 
audit purposes. They automate many aspects of development workflows, 
increasing efficiency and productivity. Overall, tracking changes through VCS 
is indispensable in modern software development, enhancing collaboration, 
reliability, and innovation. 
 
Types of VCS Evolution 
 
VCS have evolved significantly over time, adapting to the changing 
requirements of software development. Following are various types of VCS: 
 
1. Local Version Control Systems (LVCS) 
This is the simplest form of VCS, where all versioning is performed on the local 
machine. Each file and its changes are tracked in a database, providing a 
basic history of modifications. 
 
Example - Revision Control System (RCS) 
 
Features: 
● Simple setup and usage. 
● No network dependency. 
● Limited to individual usage, not suitable for collaboration. 
 
 
2. Centralized Version Control Systems (CVCS) 
A single server contains all the versioned files and clients check out files from 
this central repository. This system facilitates better management and control 
over changes. 
 
Examples - Concurrent Versions System (CVS), Subversion (SVN), and Perforce 
 
Features: 
● Enhanced collaboration capabilities 
● Centralized control and management 
● Users must be connected to the central server to commit changes 
● Potential single point of failure 
 
3. Distributed Version Control Systems (DVCS) 
Each client has a complete copy of the repository, including its full history. This 
allows for greater flexibility, such as offline work and easier branching and 
merging. 
 
Examples - Git, Mercurial, and Bazaar 
 
Features: 
● Full repository history on each client 
● Decentralized approach enhances reliability 
● Better support for complex workflows, including branching and merging

● Offline work capabilities

Common Terminologies in VCS 
 
Let us discuss the common terminologies used in VCS. 
 
Repository 
A repository or repo in a VCS is a storage space where a user's project resides. 
It contains user's project files and the entire history of changes made to those 
files. It allows the user to organize and manage their codebase. 
 
Commit 
A commit is a snapshot of a repository at a specific point in time. Each commit 
records changes to the files and includes a message describing what was 
changed and why. It helps the user keep track of the development history and 
allows the user to revert to previous states if required. 
 
Cloning 
Cloning is the process of creating a local copy of a remote or cloud based 
repository. It enables the user to work on a project locally, making changes 
and committing them before pushing them back to the remote repository. 
 
  
© Aptech Limited 
 
Branch 
A branch is a separate line of development within a repository. It allows the 
user to work on new features, bug fixes, or experiments independently from the 
main codebase. It facilitates parallel development and makes it easier for the 
user to manage multiple features or versions of a project. 
 
Checkout 
Checkout is the process of switching between different branches or commits 
in a repository. It allows the user to view and work on the code from a specific 
branch or commit. 
 
Fetching 
Fetching is the process of downloading updates from a remote repository to a 
local repository without merging them. It keeps the user's local repository up to 
date with the remote repository’s history and changes. 
 
Pulling 
Pulling is the process of fetching changes from a remote repository and 
merging them into a local repository. It integrates updates from the remote 
repository into the user's current branch, ensuring the user has the latest 
changes. 
 
Forking 
Forking is the process of creating a personal copy of someone else's repository 
on the VCS. It allows the user to freely experiment with changes without 
affecting the original project. The user can also submit pull requests to suggest 
changes to the original repository. 
 
What are Git and GitHub? 
 
Git 
Git is a distributed VCS that allows multiple developers to work on a project 
simultaneously without interfering with each other's changes.  
 
GitHub 
GitHub is a Web-based platform that provides hosting for Git repositories, along 
with additional features to facilitate collaboration and project management.  
 
Significance of Git and GitHub in Version Control 
 
Git is designed to handle everything from small to very large projects with 
speed and efficiency. It allows multiple developers to work on the same project 
independently without interfering with each other's work. 
 
  
© Aptech Limited 
 
A few of its features are as follows: 
 
 
Benefits: 
● Local Repositories: Each developer has a complete local copy of the 
repository, including the entire history. This means developers can work 
offline and have all the tools they require. 
● Distributed Nature:  Being a DVCS, Git's distributed nature improves 
collaboration by eliminating a single point of failure and allowing 
decentralized development. 
● Robust Branching:  The ability to create, switch, and merge branches 
seamlessly enables developers to experiment, isolate work, and 
integrate changes efficiently. This flexibility enhances productivity and 
code quality. 
 
GitHub provides a collaborative environment for developers to host and 
manage their code repositories. 
 
A few of its features are as follows: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
 
 
 
Branching 
Git supports branches, which allow developers to create separate lines 
of development. This feature makes it easy to work on multiple features 
or fixes simultaneously. 
Merging 
Merging in Git combines changes from different branches. Git's merging 
capabilities are robust, allowing for conflict resolution if changes collide. 
Lightweight 
Git operations are performed locally, which makes them fast and 
efficient. The local repository setup also makes Git lightweight in terms 
of resource usage. 
Speed 
Git is optimized for performance, handling large projects with speed. 
Operations such as committing, branching, and merging are swift 
contributing to a smooth workflow. 
 
 
 
Collaboration 
Tools 
GitHub offers features such as pull requests, issues, and discussions 
that facilitate collaboration among developers. Pull requests allow 
developers to propose changes, review code, and discuss 
modifications before merging them into the main branch. 
Hosting of 
Repositories 
GitHub hosts Git repositories in the cloud making them accessible 
from anywhere. This is particularly useful for open -source projects 
and distributed teams. 
© Aptech Limited 
 
Importance: 
● Community Support: GitHub has a vast community of developers who 
contribute to open -source projects, provide support, and share 
knowledge. This community -driven aspect accelerates learning and 
problem-solving. 
● Ease of Sharing Code: GitHub simplifies the process of sharing code with 
others. Developers can easily clone repositories, meaning they can 
create local copies of code repositories from platforms such as Git and 
GitHub to contribute to projects and collaborate with peers, fostering an 
environment of collective development. 
● Integration with CI/CD Tools:  GitHub integrates seamlessly with 
Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) tools, enabling 
automated testing, deployment, and monitoring of code. This 
integration streamlines the development workflow and ensures code 
quality.

● Visit the official Git Website, https://git-scm.com/. 
● Click the Download button to download the Git installer for Windows.

Step 2: Run the installer.  
 
Follow the installation prompts: 
● Locate the downloaded Git installer file (for example, Git -2.x.x-64-
bit.exe) and double-click to run it.

Configuration Choice for Downloading Git 
 
● Follow the installation wizard.  
● Click Finish button when completed. 
 
 
 
Finishing Installation of Git

Step 1: Open Git Bash (right -click the desktop or in any folder and select Git 
Bash Here) 
 
Step 2: Set the username and email address (these details will be used for the 
commits)

git config --global user.name "Peter" 
git config --global user.email peter@example.com 
 
These configuration commands set up Git with Peter’s personal information, 
which will be included in their commits. This ensures that contributions are 
correctly attributed to Peter. 
 
Installing GitHub Desktop 
Step 1: Download GitHub Desktop from the official Website. 
● Visit the URL https://desktop.github.com/ which is the official 
GitHub Desktop Website. 
● Click the Download for Windows button to download the installer. 
 
Step 2: Run the installer and follow the installation prompts. 
● Locate the downloaded GitHub Desktop installer file (for example, 
GitHubDesktopSetup.exe) and double-click to run it. 
● Follow the installation wizard. The installation process is 
straightforward and does not require many configurations. 
 
Step 3: Sign in to GitHub or create a new account. 
● After installation, launch GitHub Desktop. 
● The user will be prompted to sign in to their GitHub account. If an 
account is not already created, a new one can be created 
directly from the application. 
 
 
Signing in to GitHub Desktop 
 
● Once signed in, the user can start cloning repositories, creating 
new ones, and managing their projects using GitHub Desktop.

Step 1: Visit the GitHub Website.

● Open the Web browser and go to https://github.com/ (GitHub Website). 
 
Step 2: Click Sign up. 
● On the GitHub home page, the user will see a Sign up button in the top-
right corner. Click it to start the registration process. 
 
Step 3: Fill in the registration form (username, email, and password). 
● Username: Choose a unique username that the user will use to log in and 
that will be visible to others on GitHub. 
● Email: Enter email address. Make sure it is an email the user has access 
to, as the user will require it to verify the GitHub account. 
 
 
Enter Email Address 
● Password: Choose a strong password for the account. GitHub will 
provide feedback on the strength of the password. 
 
Step 4: Verify email address. 
● After filling out the registration form and clicking Create account, GitHub 
will send a verification email to the email address provided. 
● Open email inbox, find the verification email from GitHub, and click the 
verification link. This will confirm the user’s email address and complete 
the initial sign-up process. 
 
Step 5: Personalize GitHub account. 
● After the email is verified, log in to GitHub.

Session 02 
Basic Git Commands and Commit 
Management 
Overview 
This session provides a concise overview of essential Git commands and 
commit management. It covers initializing and cloning repositories, checking 
status, staging files, committing changes, and managing branches.  
 
Learning Objectives 
In this session, students will learn to: 
 
● List and describe basic Git commands 
● Explain branch management 
● Outline synchronization between local and remote repositories 
Basic Git Commands 
 
Git is a powerful VCS that helps developers manage their codebases. 
 
Following are some essential Git commands that developer should know: 
● git init: Initializes a new Git repository in the current directory. It creates  
a '.git' subdirectory, which contains all the necessary files for the 
repository. 
When beginning work on a new project and wanting to start tracking it with 
Git, the user uses git init  to initialize a repository in the project's root 
directory. Alternatively, If there is already a repository, but the user wants to 
ensure it is properly set up, the user can run git init again. This is useful for 
reconfiguring or confirming the repository's setup. 
 

© Aptech Limited 
 
Consider an example. Assume a folder named JohnRePpo is created.  
Within that folder, launch Command Prompt and type following command: 
 
      git init 
 
Command Execution: The command git init is executed in the directory 
C:\Newrepo\Johnrepo. 
 
Result: The message indicates a Git repository is now initialized in this 
directory.  
 
Repository Location: The '.git' directory, which stores all the configuration 
and metadata for the repository, is located in 
C:\Newrepo\Johnrepo/.git/. 
 
Thereafter, give git init command again in the same folder: 
 
 
Use of Git Init to Reinitialize a Repository 
 
Command Execution: The command git init is executed in the directory 
C:\Newrepo\Johnrepo. 
 
Result: The message indicates that there was already a Git repository 
initialized in this directory. By running git init  again, Git reinitialized the 
existing repository. 
 
Repository Location: The '.git' directory, which stores all the configuration 
and metadata for the repository, is located in 
C:\Newrepo\Johnrepo/.git/. 
 
● git clone : Copies an existing Git repository from a remote server to the 
user local machine. This command creates a local copy of the repository, 
complete with all its history and branches. 
 
When the user wants to work on a project that is hosted on a remote server, 
git clone is used to create a local copy of the repository. This includes all 
the files, history, and branches from the remote repository. 
 
Consider an example. Assume that a GitHub repository has been created 
at https://github.com/John986-creator/Johnrepo 

© Aptech Limited 
 
 
 
Use of Git Clone 
 
Command Execution:  The command git clone  
https://github.com/John986-creator/Johnrepo is executed in the 
directory 'C:\Newrepo\Johnrepo'. 
 
Cloning Process: 
o Initialization: Git starts the process of cloning the repository named 
'Johnrepo' from the given URL. 
o Object Enumeration:  Git enumerates objects, which means it 
counts the objects to be cloned. 
o Object Counting:  Git counts the total number of objects to be 
cloned (12 in this case). 
o Object Compression: Git compresses the objects for transfer. 
o Object Transfer: Git transfers the compressed objects to the local 
machine. 
o Delta Resolution: Git resolves any differences (deltas) between the 
transferred objects. 
Result: The repository is successfully cloned into the local directory 
'C:\Newrepo\Johnrepo'. 
 
● git add: Stages changes in the user working directory for the next commit. 
The user can add individual files or all changes at once. 
When the user makes changes to files in the working directory, they use 
'git add' to stage these changes. Staging is the process of preparing the 
files to be committed to the repository. 
 
s: git add <file-name> 
 
Following example demonstrates usage of the command: 
 
 
Use of Git Add 

© Aptech Limited 
 
Command Execution:  The command 'git add 'Readme.txt'  is 
executed in the directory C:\Newrepo\Johnrepo. 
 
Action: This command stages the Readme.txt file, adding it to the 
staging area in preparation for the next commit. 
 
● git commit: Records changes to the repository with a descriptive message. 
This command captures a snapshot of the project's current state. 
After staging changes using git add, the user uses git commit to record 
these changes in the repository, creating a new snapshot of the project's 
state. 
 
Syntax: git commit -m <User commit message> 
 
Following example demonstrates usage of the command: 
 
 
Use of Git Commit 
Staging a File: 
o The command git add Readme.txt  is executed to stage the 
Readme.txt file. 
 
Committing the Changes: 
o The command 'git commit -m "Hello World"' is executed to 
commit the staged changes with the message 'Hello World'. 
Result of Commit: 
o Commit Hash: '[Hello 7b8bd4f]' indicates the commit hash, which 
is a unique identifier for this commit. 
o Commit Message: 'Hello World' is the message associated with the 
commit. 
o File Change Summary: 
● '1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)': Indicates that one file was 
changed with one insertion. 
 
● 'create mode 160000 Johnrepo': Indicates the creation of a 
new mode, though this specific output might be a bit 
unusual and could relate to a specific type of file or 
repository setup. 
 

© Aptech Limited 
 
● git status : Displays the state of the working directory and the staging 
area. It shows which changes have been staged, which have not, and 
which files are not being tracked by Git. The git status command is used 
to get information about the current branch, staged changes, unstaged 
changes, and untracked files. 
Following example demonstrates usage of the command: 
 
 
 
Use of Git Status 
 
Command Execution: The command 'git status' is executed in the 
directory 'C:\Newrepo\Johnrepo'. 
 
Branch Information: 
o On branch Hello: Indicates that the user is currently on the Hello 
branch. 
 
Commit Information: 
o No commits yet: Indicates that there have been no commits 
made to this branch yet. 
 
● git log : Shows the commit history for the current branch. It provides 
information about each commit, such as the author, date, and commit 
message. The git log command is used to view the history of commits in 
the current branch, providing details about each commit. 
Following example demonstrates usage of the command: 
 
 
 
Use of Git Log 
 
Command Execution:  The command git log  is executed in the 
directory 'C:\Newrepo\Johnrepo'. 
 
Commit Information: 
o Commit Hash: '7b8bd4fbd531e7a687fda822c5bdd4fbbe4e1486' is 
the unique identifier for this commit. 
o Branch and HEAD: '(HEAD -> Hello)' indicates that this commit is the 
HEAD of the Hello branch, meaning it is the latest commit on this 
branch. 

© Aptech Limited 
 
o Author: 'John986-creator <… @gmail.com>' is the author of the 
commit. 
o Date: 'Fri Jul 5 23:48:19 2024 +0530' is the date and time when the 
commit was made. 
o Commit Message: 'Hello World' is the message provided during the 
commit. 
 
● git diff : Compares changes between commits, the working directory, 
and the staging area. This command helps the user see what has changed 
in the user codebase. The git diff  command is used to see what has 
changed in the working directory compared to the staging area or the 
latest commit. This helps the user review modifications before staging or 
committing them. 
Syntax: git diff 
 
Following example demonstrates usage of the command: 
 
 
 
Use of Git Diff 
 
Command Execution: The command git diff is executed in the  
directory 'C:\Newrepo\Johnrepo'. 
 
Output: No differences are shown in the output, indicating that there are no  
changes between the working directory and the staging area or the latest  
commit. 
● git branch : Lists all branches in the repository and indicates the current 
branch. The user can also create and delete branches with this command.  
The git branch  commands are used to manage branches in the 
repository, allowing the user to create new branches for different features 
or tasks, switch between branches, and delete branches when they are no 
longer required. 
 
Syntax: 
git branch 
git branch <branch-name> 
git branch -d <branch-name> 
 
  

© Aptech Limited 
 
Following example demonstrates usage of these commands: 
 
 
 
Use of Git Branch 
 
List Branches: 
● The command git branch is executed to list all branches in the 
repository. 
● Output:   
'* Hello': Indicates that Hello is the current branch. 
'main': Indicates another branch present in the repository. 
 
Create a New Branch: 
● The command git branch Boom  is executed to create a new 
branch named 'Boom'. 
Delete a Branch: 
● The command git branch -d Boom  is executed to delete the 
branch named 'Boom'. 
● Output: 'Deleted branch Boom (was 7b8bd4f)'. 
 
Confirms that the branch Boom is deleted and provides the last commit 
hash of that branch. 
● git checkout : Switches between branches or restores working directory 
files. The user can utilize this command to browse the project's history or 
switch to a different branch.  
Syntax: git checkout <branch-name> 
 
The git branch  and git checkout  commands are used to manage 
branches in the repository, allowing the user to create new branches for 
different features or tasks, switch between branches, and delete branches 
when they are no longer required. 
  

© Aptech Limited 
 
Following example demonstrates usage of these commands: 
 
 
 
Use of Git Checkout 
 
Switch to a Branch: 
● The command git checkout Hello  is executed to switch to the 
'Hello' branch. 
● Output: Already on 'Hello' indicates that the user is already on the 
Hello branch. 
● git merge : Integrates changes from one branch into another. This 
command helps combine different lines of development. This command is 
useful in merging branches. To merge changes from one branch into the 
current branch, the user requirements to specify the branch name they 
want to merge. 
Syntax: git merge <branch-name> 
 
 
 
Use of Git Merge 
 
Command Execution: The command 'git merge rebase.txt'  is 
executed in the directory 'C:\Newrepo\Johnrepo'. 
 
● git pull : Fetches changes from a remote repository and merges them 
into the user's current branch. It combines git fetch  and git merge  in 
one step. 
Syntax: git pull <remote> <branch> 
 
  

© Aptech Limited 
 
Following example demonstrates usage of the command: 
 
 
Use of Git Pull 
 
Synchronizing Local Repository: The git pull command is used to update 
the local repository with changes from the remote repository. It combines 
git fetch (to fetch changes) and git merge (to merge changes) in one 
step. 
 
Command Execution: The command git pull origin main is executed 
in the directory 'C:\Newrepo\Johnrepo'. 
 
Fetching Changes: 
o The output indicates that Git is fetching changes from the remote 
repository at https://github.com/John986-creator/Johnrepo. 
o '* branch main -> FETCH_HEAD': This indicates that the main branch 
from the remote repository is being fetched.

Types of Automated Testing: 
 
⮚ Unit Testing 
 
Unit Testing is automated testing that focuses on individual units or 
components of a software application. The goal is to validate that each 
software unit performs as expected. A unit is the smallest testable part of an 
application, often a function or method. 
 
Characteristics: Listed are several essential characteristics of unit testing in 
continuous integration: 
● Isolated: Each unit test focuses on a single function or method, ensuring 
the component is tested independently of other application parts. 
● Fast: Unit tests are generally quick to execute, making running them 
frequently during development feasible. 
● Frequent Execution: Developers often run unit tests as part of their regular 
workflow to catch and fix errors early in development. 
● Simple: Unit tests are usually simple to write and maintain, focusing on 
testing specific inputs and outputs. 
● Mocking/Stubbing: Unit tests often use mocks or stubs to simulate 
interactions with external dependencies (For example, databases and 
APIs). 
 
Tools: JUnit (Java), NUnit (.NET), PyTest (Python), Jest (JavaScript). 
 
⮚ Integration Testing 
 
Integration Testing is the phase of testing in which individual units are 
combined and tested as a group. The goal is to expose defects in the 
interaction between integrated units or components. 
 
Characteristics: These are some important characteristics of integration 
testing in continuous integration: 
● Combines Units: Integration tests focus on interactions between multiple 
components or modules, ensuring they work together correctly. 
● Medium Scope:  These tests cover more significant parts of the 
application than unit tests but are more focused than end-to-end tests. 
● Interface Testing: Integration tests validate that the interfaces between 
components are functioning as expected. 
● Incremental Testing:  Integration can be tested incrementally by 
combining components step-by-step or all at once (big bang). 
● Realistic Scenarios: Tests often simulate real-world interactions between 
components, uncovering issues that may not be apparent in isolated 
unit tests.

● Incremental: Testing components incrementally as they are

⮚ End-to-End Testing 
 
End-to-End Testing (E2E) is a type of testing that validates the entire software 
application flow from start to finish. The goal is to simulate real user scenarios 
and validate the systems complete integration and data integrity. 
 
Characteristics: These are several key characteristics of end -to-end testing 
in continuous integration: 
● Comprehensive: E2E tests validate the complete flow of the application 
from start to finish, covering the entire stack. 
● User-Centric: These tests simulate real user scenarios, ensuring that the 
application behaves as expected from the users perspective. 
● High-Level: E2E tests cover broad scenarios including user interactions, 
UI behavior, and backend processing. 
● Complex: These tests are typically more complex to write and maintain 
due to the requirements to simulate realistic user interactions and handle 
various dependencies. 
● Time-Consuming: E2E tests can take longer to execute than unit or 
integration tests, but they provide valuable feedback on the overall 
application behavior. 
● Environment Dependent:  These tests often require a fully deployed 
environment including databases, servers, and external services. 
Tools: Selenium, Cypress, Puppeteer.

Key Concepts of IaC 
 
The most important key concepts of IaC are: 
1. Declarative vs. Imperative Approach: 
⮚ Declarative: Specifies the desired end state of the infrastructure. 
Tools such as Terraform and CloudFormation use a declarative 
approach, where users define what they want the infrastructure 
to look like, and the tool takes care of creating and maintaining 
that state. 
⮚ Imperative: Specifies the exact steps required to achieve the 
desired state. Tools such as Ansible and Chef can be used 
imperatively, where the user defines the step -by-step process to 
reach the desired configuration. 
 
 
2. Version Control: 
⮚ IaC allows users to store configuration files in version control 
systems (For example, Git). This provides a history of changes, 
facilitates collaboration, and enables rollback to previous 
configurations if required. 
3. Idempotence: 
⮚ Idempotence ensures that applying the same configuration 
multiple times results in the same state. This is crucial for reliable 
and repeatable deployments. 
4. Modularity: 
⮚ IaC encourages the use of reusable modules or components. This 
allows for easier management and scaling of infrastructure 
components.

Rollback strategies are crucial for reverting deployments when issues arise, 
ensuring that systems can return to a stable state. Let us go over some key

• Version Control Rollback: 
This method involves rolling back to a previous version of the codebase 
using version control systems similar to Git. It is one of the simplest 
rollback strategies and works well for code-level issues. 
• Feature Toggles: 
Feature toggles allow you to enable or disable specific features without 
redeploying code. This strategy provides flexibility by quickly turning off 
problematic features in production environments. 
• Blue-Green Deployment: 
In this strategy, two identical environments (blue and green) are 
maintained. When an issue occurs, traffic is switched back to the 
previous environment (blue), while the problematic environment 
(green) is fixed. 
 
• Canary Deployment: 
Canary deployment gradually introduces new changes to a small 
subset of users. If issues are detected, you can easily rollback the 
deployment before it affects the majority of users.

Using slide 19, explain different types of backup strategies and discuss their

Say: 
Backup strategies are essential for ensuring data integrity and availability in 
the event of data loss. Let us explore the four main types of backup strategies: 
• Full Backup: 
A full backup creates a complete copy of all data. It is the most 
comprehensive backup but can take longer and require more storage 
space. Full backups are typically used periodically. 
• Incremental Backup: 
Incremental backups only back up data that has changed since the 
last backup, making it faster and more storage-efficient. This strategy is 
often used daily in combination with periodic full backups. 
• Differential Backup: 
A differential backup captures all changes made since the last full 
backup. While it requires more space than an incremental backup, it 
simplifies the restoration process since only two backup sets (the full 
backup and differential backup) are required. 
• Snapshot Backup: 
Snapshot backups create an image of the system at a specific point in 
time. It is commonly used for virtual machines or cloud environments 
where fast recovery and minimal downtime are required.
